name: Edward VI of England
summary: Edward VI inherited the English and Irish crowns as a child and governed with a council. In his own papers he pressed for Protestant worship and royal oversight of the church, and proposed limits on the concentration of wealth and farmland. In 1553 he sought to redirect the hereditary succession to Lady Jane Grey.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Edward used his 1553 Devise to keep the crown within a specified hereditary line, ultimately naming his cousin Lady Jane Grey and her male heirs.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: His Discourse treats paid service and work for wages as continuing parts of a well-ordered commonwealth, with servants expected to work diligently for their masters and households expected to pay for that service.

capital-controls.rationale: He drafted an act making carrying bullion out of the realm a felony, listed conveying bullion and goods abroad among the commonwealth's sores, and proposed prohibiting export of horses.

character-from-environment.rationale: Discourse: quoting Horace's image of the new vessel keeping the savour of what it was first filled with, he says 'for the most part men be as they be brought up', and makes good education the first remedy. A pair of school orations argues both sides of whether people are evil by nature.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Edward’s Discourse assigns church discipline in each diocese to bishops selected for their fitness and commissioned to exercise it.

class-collaboration.rationale: His Discourse lists 'engendering friendship in all the parts of the commonwealth' as a remedy and describes gentlemen, merchants, artisans and husbandmen as limbs that must each use their gain so the others can do their service.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: His Discourse lists excess in apparel, diet and building among the sores of the commonwealth, and he wrote a bill restraining dress by rank.

country-wealth-only-from-land.rationale: His Discourse treats merchants and artisans as essential to sustaining the commonwealth and calls on merchants to enrich its supply by bringing in goods from abroad.

death-penalty.rationale: In his January 1552 memorandum on Somerset and his confederates, Edward called for punishment and execution according to law to secure the realm and set an example.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Edward used his 1553 Devise to settle the crown on Lady Jane Grey and her male heirs, preserving transmission from parent to child within the line he designated.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: In his journal for 15 April 1552, Edward says he commissioned the chancellor, bishops and peers to dissolve Parliament when illness prevented him from attending.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: In his Discourse, Edward expressly allows people to keep sheep in limited numbers and expects husbandmen to sell meat and dairy products as part of their vocation.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: In his autograph conclusion of September 1552, Edward supported seeking a treaty with the Emperor and other princes before taking up joint action against France in the dispute over aid to the Emperor.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: Edward approved specified silver fineness for different denominations in 1551 and personally directed the mint to add two denominations at the fine silver standard.

more-religion-public.rationale: Edward personally intervened to enforce conformity to statutory Protestant worship in Mary’s household and refused the imperial ambassador’s request to exempt her.

national-church-status.rationale: When Mary sought to retain the Mass in her household, Edward required obedience to the statutory service of the national church.

pay-off-national-debt.rationale: The third clause of the draft will directs the executors to pursue existing measures and find further means for prompt repayment of the Crown’s debts. The minutes survive in Secretary Petre’s hand.

property-fundamental.rationale: In his Discourse and draft acts he would cap holdings (two farms, 2,000 sheep, ceilings on wealth by occupation) and he wants forfeitures from those who have 'devoured their neighbours', which treats property rights as limited by the commonwealth.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Discourse: it is convenient to enrich the country but hurtful to enrich any one part immoderately, and no person may have more than the commonwealth can bear.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Edward personally rejected an exemption for Mary’s Mass and required her to obey the worship prescribed by statute, giving the established Protestant service legal precedence.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Edward told Mary that she must obey the statute on worship as a subject and refused the imperial ambassador’s request to let her retain the Mass.

separate-church-state.rationale: Edward personally intervened to enforce the statutory form of public worship when Mary continued hearing Mass and the imperial ambassador sought an exemption for her.

state-harmful.rationale: Edward’s Discourse prescribes a single governor and a common law, with duly authorised officials enforcing it throughout the realm.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: His Discourse proposes public measures to train young people in trades, encourage upright conduct and enforce penalties for conduct he regarded as vicious.

students-direct-own-learning.rationale: His Discourse proposes directing children into trades through compulsory parental instruction in the family trade or apprenticeships arranged in towns.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: In his own hand he listed gathering and coining church plate, selling chantry and college lands, and having patrons and clergy bound by statute (no reserving of benefice income, no church leases beyond 21 years). He also wanted discipline exercised only by bishops he picked and commissioned.

taxation-theft.rationale: In his autograph Memorial as to Ways and Means, Edward identifies a parliamentary subsidy as part of his preferred plan to repay the Crown’s foreign debts.

notes: This pass checked government and the succession, religion and civil liberty, economic regulation and debt, education and work, and war and diplomacy in the two volumes of Literary Remains and the Inner Temple succession record. The journal distinguishes some personal acts from reported council and parliamentary business. The will’s defensive-war instruction applies expressly during a successor’s minority. The Discourse proposes limits on accumulated wealth and holdings, rather than a ceiling on annual income. School declamations were checked as assignments rather than treated as personal commitments. Follow-up on the widest lines checked the Boulogne and Scottish negotiations and the September 1552 memorandum on aid to the Emperor. Edward’s own conclusion addresses proposed joint action against France. His ceremonial ratification of the Boulogne peace supplies no personal position on territorial expansion. Searches in the letters and political papers covered alliances, borders, language and nationality, and the Discourse was checked for rank, labour and local government. Challis’s edition of the Pekham letter documents Edward’s personal coinage instructions.
